Vignette:
# Mariana

Mariana was twenty-two years old when the bomb went off at the outdoor market in her neighbourhood. She had gone early that Saturday morning to buy ingredients for her mother's birthday dinner—cilantro, lime, the good kind of chorizo from the vendor she trusted. The market was crowded, the way it always was on weekends, vendors calling out prices, children running between the stalls, the smell of grilled corn and fresh flowers mixing in the warm air. She was standing near the produce section, reaching for avocados, when the sound came—not a sound she could describe even now, two years later. She knows something exploded. She knows people screamed. But the moments between the flash and waking up on the ground are simply gone, erased from her memory as though they never happened. When she tries to reconstruct what occurred, she hits a wall of blankness. Part of her has always needed to know exactly what she saw, what she did, whether she helped anyone or just lay there—but that knowledge is locked away somewhere she cannot reach.

What Mariana does remember is the hospital, the bandages on her left arm, the way her hands shook for hours. She remembers her mother's face. And she remembers, with a clarity that feels almost obscene given the gaps elsewhere, the moment she understood that the world was not what she had believed it to be. Before that Saturday, she had assumed safety was something that simply existed if you were careful, if you stayed in familiar places, if you kept to routine. Now she knew better. Danger lived in ordinary moments. It lived in markets and crowds and the spaces where people gathered. There was no formula that could protect her.

The rage came later, building slowly over the first weeks and then arriving with full force. When she allowed herself to think about what happened—which she tried not to do—fury would flood through her, hot and undirected, leaving her shaking and sometimes unable to move for hours afterward. She could not articulate why the rage felt so necessary, only that when she tried to talk about the event, the words simply would not come. She knew what had happened. Her body knew. But her mouth could not form the sentences. So she stopped trying.

Within months, Mariana had constructed a careful architecture of avoidance. She quit her first job at a retail store because the fluorescent lights and the crowds made her chest tight, and because she could not bear the way customers would move suddenly around her—reaching past her for merchandise, tapping her shoulder to ask questions. Every unexpected movement sent her into a state of immediate alarm, her body flooding with the certainty that danger was coming. She found work at a warehouse on the outskirts of the city, where she could control her environment more carefully. The job was solitary, the aisles long and predictable, and she could see people coming from far away. But even there, she positioned herself so her back was always to a wall. She scanned the space constantly, noting exits, watching for sudden motion. Her supervisor had begun to comment that she seemed "tense," that she didn't make eye contact during their brief check-ins. She had come to believe that meeting someone's eyes was dangerous—that it created a vulnerability she could not afford.

At night, safety felt like a fiction. Mariana would lie awake for hours, her body rigid, listening to sounds in her apartment that she could not identify. She tried to sleep but found herself deliberately leaving her body instead, a dissociation so complete that she would sometimes lose hours without knowing where the time had gone. It was easier than being present in the dark, easier than feeling the way her body betrayed her by remaining vigilant even when her mind begged for rest.

Two months ago, Mariana's mother had finally confronted her directly. She had noticed her daughter's weight loss, the dark circles, the way Mariana flinched at the slightest noise. She had watched her avoid family gatherings, decline invitations, sit at the dinner table with her eyes fixed on her plate. When her mother reached across the table to touch her hand, Mariana had jerked away so violently that she knocked over a glass. In that moment, seeing her mother's hurt, something shifted. Mariana realized that the world she had been trying to make safe through constant vigilance and avoidance was becoming smaller every day. She was exhausted. She was alone. And she was beginning to suspect that her body, which she had learned to fear and distrust, might be the only thing that could help her find her way back.
